- Intro to History of Science: Crash Course History of Science #1: Kind: captions Language: en Hello, and welcome to our new series—Crash Course: History of Science. My name is Hank Green, and I’ve wanted to produce this course for years. I’m obsessed with how people throughout the ages have uncovered truths about the universe and converted these into a wealth of technological wonders. This process has decreased the suffering of millions of humans—even as it’s sparked entirely new problems. Regardless of the outcomes of scientific inquiry, the process itself is fascinating. The world you inhabit today is full of gadgets that once belonged to science fiction. We can model what the earth looked like millions of years ago, or zoom in and observe the atoms that make up our own bodies. We are going to tell that inspiring story: we’ll be thinking about thinking with Aristotle, digging canals in Song Dynasty China, listening to robot musicians in medieval Turkey, fighting an electrical war in New York City, and discovering the shape of DNA in Cold War England. But the history of science is not only a story of humanity’s collective movement from ignorance to knowledge, for two different reasons. First, as much as scientists today may not like to admit it, we are still pretty ignorant… And we don’t agree on what it would mean to reach the ultimate Truth, capital T. Take a big question that we've been asking for a long time like “what is stuff”: While modern physicists will tell you that stuff is made of atoms, and atoms are made of quarks and leptons, we still don’t know why quarks exist. Or why there appears to be far more matter in the universe than we can account for. Even something as basic as “stuff” needs a lot more sciencing! Second, and more importantly for historians, “science” isn’t a stable or single idea. That’s why, in this episode, we’re going to be thinking about some ways to answer a deceptively simple question: what is the history of science the history of? [intro music plays] Today, “science” can mean both our body of knowledge about the world as well as the methods we use to create that knowledge, or how we know the stuff that we know. Within that “how,” there are two main practices—things that we do—that systematically generate knowledge: One: observe some specific aspect of the world. For example, Darwin spent decades obsessively observing the subtle variations in different kinds of barnacles, orchids, turtles, birds, and other living things. This led him to theorize how they had changed over time. My dude loved barnacles! Two: conduct an experiment to answer some question about the world. Did Galileo drop two metal balls of different masses from the Leaning Tower of Pisa, to show that they fall at the same rate and disprove Aristotle’s theory of gravity? Probably not. But Dutch thinkers Simon Stevin and Jan Cornets de Groot did conduct that experiment soon after. Today, we have much bigger “towers” for testing theories in physics: the Large Hadron Collider is seventeen miles long! Finally, when I said systematically, I meant that there are rules about observing or experimenting—rules that anyone can follow. That notion of anyone being able to be a scientist is super important. In fact, a lot of contemporary scientists have three Latin words tattooed on their arms: “NULLIUS IN VERBA”—“on no one’s word…” Let’s explore this phrase because it's important. In this series, The Thoughtbubble is going to bring to life different wonders from the history of science. Today, our wonder is pretty abstract: the wonder of the reproducible experiment. “NULLIUS IN VERBA” is the motto of the Royal Society. This group of knowledge-makers was founded in 1660 as a “College for the Promoting of Physico-Mathematical Experimental Learning” and re-founded in 1663 as “the Royal Society of London for the Improvement of Natural Knowledge.” And it’s still around today! The Society was started as a place to debate new ideas about nature. Its members demonstrated experiments in front of each other—“witnessing” the proofs behind their theories. They wrote up these theories in the Society’s Philosophical Transactions, one of the world’s oldest peer-reviewed scientific journals. Influenced by Francis Bacon’s ideas, which would eventually become associated with the “scientific method,” the founding members of the Royal Society chose a motto with an unambiguous meaning: don’t believe something just because someone tells you it’s true. Test out each new hypothesis, or educated guess, yourself. In other words: your individual proof of how some natural phenomenon works should be something that anyone can reproduce. This idea had an enormous impact on the history of science. Later members of the Royal Society included stars such as Ike Newton, Ben Franklin, Mike Faraday, Chuck Darwin, and even Big Al Einstein, who was about as British as sauerkraut. In fact—plot twist!—the early scientists who adopted the creed “NULLIUS IN VERBA” were not actually “scientists.” They were well-off alchemists and medical doctors, and they called themselves Natural Philosophers. Or, "People who loved truths concerning the world around them." Natural philosophy in seventeenth-century England was sort of like the contemporary natural sciences mashed up with medicine, mathematics, some philosophy–philosophy, and a whiff of religion. The word “scientist” was only coined recently, in historical terms, in the 1830s, and caught on around 1840. It was made up by an English scientist named William Whewell who was also a historian of science and a priest. So if we only cared about the history of people called “scientists,” our job would be easy: there aren’t any until around 1840! And most people called scientists, or natural philosophers, looked suspiciously similar to one another. Take the Royal Society: its members have been, until recently, almost exclusively rich English men. Even though their ranks have included many incredibly clever scientists, they haven’t represented anything like all knowledge makers. The sixty-second President of the Royal Society, biophysicist Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, is the group’s first non-white leader. And there has never been a female President. But the history of systematically knowing stuff goes back much further than the Royal Society and includes more types of people than English blokes. Thus “science” is a historical and social concept—not one that’s existed forever, in the same way for all people. Because the history of science includes many systems of understanding the world, we have to consider these systems on their own terms. It may seem simpler to focus on the “winners” of history. But hearing only the big Euroamerican names—Plato, Einstein—doesn’t teach us as much about our global system of science today. Taking the time to highlight different knowledge worlds will help us see our own as relatively recent, not entirely unified, and evolving. For example, we’ll learn about the Greco-Latin-Jewish-Arabic medicine of the medieval Mediterranean world, millennia of ayurvedic knowledge across the Subcontinent, traditional Chinese medicine, and Incan “talking knots” and engineering—just to name a few. Each of these systems has its own social norms about what count as valid ways to make and share knowledge. We’ll look at modern scientific norms in a later episode. And each of these can help us see the “otherness” of these past or different cultures as not so other, after all. We can see natural philosophers and other proto-scientists as smart people making sense of their world, not as “bad” scientists. They understood the world around them in the smartest way they could. For example, according to medieval Mediterranean medicine, the organ in my head was for venting waste heat, not thinking. People in the past weren’t stupid: they knew that if your head was chopped off, that was curtains for you. They just weren’t sure what all this weird gray stuff did. Even today—though we can see a neuron fire in high-resolution—we struggle to understand what really goes on when it fires, that is, the role a single neuron plays in thinking… much less answer the question, what is consciousness. The history of science really gets even juicier when incremental, nagging questions about the natural world add up and cause a scientific discipline, or an entire society, to change in a “revolutionary” way. Later in the series, we’ll look at moments of revolution within the sciences alongside philosophers such as Thomas Kuhn and Michel Foucault, who... did not always agree. They show that science isn’t only historical and social, but constructs entire worlds of knowledge in which we all find ourselves trapped. But don’t worry about that just yet. By learning the history of science, we will automatically start to think about our own knowledge world as historical—not finished, not capital-E enlightened. Around the world, humans are still actively working to understand our universe… but they don’t all agree on how to do it. We may be able to make more accurate models of natural phenomena… but we may never find the ultimate answers we seek. At its limit, the history of science touches on the study of religion: the diverse and changing nature of the never-ending human search for Truth, capital T. Our path through past knowledge worlds is going to be a beautiful and powerful one. There are many, many marvelous insights to celebrate. To help us keep our footing as we jump across centuries and continents, we’re going to keep our eyes on five big questions. Questions that, to this day, we do not have complete answers to. First: what is stuff? From atoms to dark matter to spacetime: what are things made of? “Things,” by the way, includes air, fire, and outer space: if you think I’m going to sit here and not celebrate the death of phlogiston with you, you’re sorely mistaken! Number two: what is Life? What’s the simplest way to define living things? Are viruses alive? Is the earth alive? Where did life come from? Where did current organisms come from? How do we understand their interactions with each other and their world? Three: where are we? What is this place, the earth? What is its place in the cosmos? Is this the only universe? Four: when are we? More questions of scale: how long have we been around? What about living things? What about the whole universe? What came before that? And five: how can we agree on what we know? And how can I convince more people that the stuff I know is accurate? For example, how can I show anti-vaccers that vaccines are necessary!? Regarding technology, how should we talk about what to do what our knowledge? All of these questions have been considered by people as far back as records exist. They also remain active areas of study today. But the last theme is so important that it gets its the final section. Humans have always tried to describe the world, for lots of reasons: in part because it’s fascinating (“magnets—how do they work!?”), and in part to control it. Knowledge, as they told us in grade school, really is power! The power that knowing stuff gives the knower is exactly why we should study the history Thus one goal of this course is to highlight how the values (beliefs about right and wrong) and ethics (acceptable behaviors) of scientists and engineers shape our world. And how, conversely, sciences and technologies are shaped by the societies that produce them. We have a responsibility as citizens to understand and to act accordingly. Our world today looks radically dissimilar to that of three hundred years ago. To quote Andy Weir, we’ve “scienced” the heck out of it. We learned about stuff, made new technologies, and are currently scrambling to learn new stuff to solve the problems that our old technologies created. Facing an utterly unprecedented total ecological catastrophe, we may need to “science” it even more, in one way or another. We’ll talk more about this in future episodes. Learning the history of science can help shine a light on this dark future. Next time—pack your spanakopita: we’re heading to ancient Greece to invent natural philosophy with the Presocratics. Until then, this has been—“on no one’s word”—Crash Course: History of Science! Crash Course History of Science is filmed in the Dr. Cheryl C. Kinney Studio in Missoula, MT and It’s made with the help of all of these nice people. And our animation team is Thought Cafe. Crash Course is a Complexly production. - The Scientific Method: Crash Course Biology #2: Kind: captions Language: en-US Science! The word comes from a Latin verb&nbsp;meaning to “know.” And don’t get me wrong: the knowing part is important. But the&nbsp;questions are where it’s really at. Curiosity about everything around us&nbsp; and within us is fuel for science’s fire. That includes big stuff like “What’s the&nbsp; universe made of?” and “Where did life begin?” But it also includes burning questions like, “Why&nbsp;does cut grass smell like watermelon?” and “How easy is it really to slip on a banana peel?” Because based on the cartoons that I saw and, uhh, lots of Mario Kart, I really thought that was&nbsp;going to be a much bigger problem in the future. Of course, there are questions&nbsp; outside the scope of science, too. Like, science can’t tell you if&nbsp;you should try and land that sweet skateboard trick. Though it can explain&nbsp;what might happen to your leg if you fail. As the science of life, biology explores the&nbsp;relationships and interactions among living things and their environment. And like all&nbsp;science, it’s built on layers of hypotheses, ideas that are tested with evidence, and what’s&nbsp;basically a big group chat spanning centuries. Hi, I’m Dr. Sammy, your friendly neighborhood&nbsp; entomologist, and this is Crash Course Biology! [THEME MUSIC] The word “scientist” has only&nbsp;existed in English since the nineteenth century. But people from&nbsp;every corner of the globe have been figuring stuff out by observing&nbsp;the physical world for a long time. For example, records of medicine and&nbsp;natural history date back hundreds and even thousands of years in ancient&nbsp;India, Greece, and China. Centuries ago, Maya astronomers precisely tracked&nbsp; the movements of the sun, moon, and planets— leaving behind calendars&nbsp;still used by their descendants today. And Indigenous cultures worldwide have developed&nbsp;rich understandings of the natural world through close observation. Like, for example,&nbsp;Indigenous Alaskans have had a front-row seat to climate change, observing thinning&nbsp;sea ice and declining salmon populations. And Aboriginal people in Australia&nbsp;told stories of “firehawks,” birds that intentionally spread fires by airdropping&nbsp; flaming sticks into brush to scare out prey, long before professional scientists&nbsp; described the behavior in 2017. As a process of discovery and knowing, science has&nbsp;been formalized with the scientific method. Maybe you’ve heard these six simple steps before. First,&nbsp;so the method goes, you make an observation that leads you to ask a question, like, “I noticed&nbsp;how my hard-boiled egg seems to retain water. I wonder what happens if I&nbsp;put it in the microwave?” Next, comes a hypothesis — a testable explanation,&nbsp; or reasonable prediction of what will&nbsp;happen. Like, “I hypothesize the water will boil inside the egg, build up&nbsp;pressure, and the egg will explode.” Next, you test that hypothesis with an experiment&nbsp;that can be repeated. You analyze the results, you report the conclusions, and finally, you&nbsp;use the conclusions to make new hypotheses. Alright, let's see... Our experiment concludes that the egg got blown&nbsp;to smithereens. 1 out of 10. Would not do again. So based on what I just observed, I now&nbsp;hypothesize that if I remove the eggshell first and then microwave the egg, pressure won’t&nbsp;build enough for it to explode. Notice here that the Scientific Method is a cycle. My starting&nbsp;hypothesis brought me around to a new one. Those six steps are an idealized&nbsp; version of the scientific method. Except the exploding part.&nbsp; Typically we don’t want that. *coughs* In the real world, science progresses less like&nbsp; a straight line from hypothesis to conclusion,&nbsp;&nbsp; and more like a bunch of looping squiggles that&nbsp;can change direction in ways&nbsp;that we don’t even see coming. It still has that same idea at heart: testing&nbsp;ideas with evidence and repeating observations to understand cause and effect. But we have to&nbsp;accept that things don’t always stick to the plan. Steps get repeated or rearranged. Experiments&nbsp;fail (and boy, don’t I know it). Scientists sometimes have to backtrack, zipping all the way&nbsp;to the beginning to gather more observations. Or some observations don’t make sense until&nbsp;other observations fill in the gaps. Like, nobody could figure out how genes encode&nbsp;proteins until the helix structure of DNA was revealed in 1953. And inevitably, answering&nbsp;one question sparks more questions. Like, okay, a hard-boiled egg explodes in the&nbsp; microwave. But what about a grape? And perhaps more importantly, what sort&nbsp; of monster eats warm grapes? *shudder* Anyway, the scientific process’s path can be&nbsp; a bit like a twisty, dynamic roller coaster. Sometimes it backs up, sometimes it changes&nbsp;direction. And occasionally there’s screaming… I’m looking at you, grad school. We’ve been conditioned by books and movies to&nbsp; imagine a solitary, genius taking this wild ride all by themself. Glasses framing their heroic&nbsp;face as they stare stoically into the distance. But actually, it’s typically teams of&nbsp;scientists riding the twists and turns&nbsp;together. They share ideas, questions,&nbsp;and evidence, thinking problems through as a group. To learn more, let’s catch&nbsp;a matinee over in the Theater of Life… By the middle of the twentieth century, biologists were starting to ask increasingly in-depth questions about life on Earth and&nbsp;how it works on a microscopic scale. But living organisms are complex… and&nbsp;can be unwieldy subjects to study. Enter the Argentinian biochemist, Dr. Luis&nbsp;Federico Leloir, alongside his team. They wondered if the building blocks of life, cells, worked the same way outside of an organism&nbsp;as they do inside. Like, if they separated&nbsp;cells from an intact organ and studied them, would the results also explain how&nbsp; cells worked inside a living thing? A huge part of what made the team successful was&nbsp;their collaboration and scrappiness. You see, the team had equipment that separates fluids by&nbsp;spinning at high speeds, called a centrifuge. But they didn’t have the funds for a refrigerated&nbsp;version. Keeping things cold was essential for separating the cell without anything degrading. But the team was crafty. They filled inner tubes from car tires with water, ice, and salt to&nbsp;create a refrigerating effect. And it worked! Being able to study a cell effectively&nbsp; outside of an organism was a big deal. It allowed scientists, including&nbsp;Leloir, to start asking way more complicated questions about the basic&nbsp;building blocks of life — which has, in turn, helped us understand more about how&nbsp; organisms work, including how to fight diseases. When Leloir won a Nobel prize in 1970, he&nbsp;credited not only the collaboration among his team, but also the ongoing collaborative&nbsp; conversation of science itself. He said “This is just one step in a much larger&nbsp;project… We hardly know even a little.” Mmm, bravo. So you can see how, in a way, all&nbsp;of science is a team effort. Teams of scientists build on other teams’ work, in what’s basically&nbsp;one big ongoing discussion, sort of like that big group text that we mentioned in the opening. Each new observation we communicate adds to the pool of collective knowledge like each text&nbsp;message building out the larger conversation. Often, a hypothesis gets tested over and over&nbsp; and over again from different angles. And then it gets linked up with other hypotheses that&nbsp;are getting tested over and over — and evidence for all of them keeps accumulating like a tiny&nbsp;snowball rolled into a massive snow-conclusion… a snow-clusion! (I’m still working on that analogy). But – anyway – that’s how you get a&nbsp;scientific theory. It’s not a theory like your neighbor’s speculation that his&nbsp;cat was King Tut in a former life. But, when we use the word “theory” in a science-y way,&nbsp; that means that the bar for evidence is high.&nbsp;&nbsp; Scientific theories are backed by strong&nbsp; consensus from the scientific community,&nbsp;&nbsp; based on a broad range of evidence. And&nbsp;theories are the basis for studying a subject. Take the Big Bang Theory: the&nbsp;idea that the universe began with a massive expansion event. There’s&nbsp;still so much to study about the theory of the big bang. Like the study of leftover&nbsp;energy from the expansion of the universe. And more and more research is being done all&nbsp;the time, spurring more testable hypotheses that add depth to the theory. New theories are always&nbsp;being revised, whenever enough new evidence piles up that doesn’t support them in their current&nbsp;state. And then there are laws: very precise, universal statements describing something&nbsp; that always happens in the physical world. For example, the first law of thermodynamics&nbsp; says energy cannot be created or destroyed. And it applies to everything, including life. Energy&nbsp;takes different forms as it passes through plants, animals, and soil, but the total amount&nbsp;of energy stays the same. For any scientific idea to become a theory or law, it needs&nbsp;to be backed by a groundswell of evidence. Scientists decide how much evidence is enough&nbsp; and what it all means through a process called peer review. Scientists will submit their&nbsp;research by writing up what they hypothesized, how they tested it, and what happened. But&nbsp;before their work makes it to the wider world, it gets checked by their peers—other&nbsp; scientists who are also experts in their field. Peer review isn’t perfect. But it’s a really&nbsp;important way of catching mistakes or even outright fraud before papers make it&nbsp;out into the wider world. That means the world’s experts on platypuses are&nbsp;discussing and reading other platypus experts’ work before it even gets published. And you can bet that group chat is fire. It’s critical that the world’s scientists&nbsp;reviewing and interpreting this research have high data literacy. That’s&nbsp;an ability to create, organize, understand, and communicate data,&nbsp;which are recorded observations. Data literacy enables scientists to design&nbsp;experiments that collect reliable data and actually answer the questions they want to ask. And when it’s time to analyze their results, it helps them accurately interpret and&nbsp;understand what the data mean— whether that’s their own research or someone else’s. And to help them interpret the data, scientists use models to try multiple&nbsp;ways of testing and understanding ideas. [upbeat music] Not that kind of model. These kinds of models. Consider the cell membrane: a thin&nbsp;layer holding together the cell’s&nbsp;squishy parts. It is possible to directly&nbsp;observe cell membranes under a microscope. Which is amazing. But there’s a&nbsp;lot happening in that tiny world: three different kinds of molecules wiggling&nbsp;in perpetual motion. And models — which are representations of scientific theories or&nbsp;processes—can help clarify what’s going on. For example, a visual model can turn a microscope&nbsp; picture into something easier to digest:&nbsp;&nbsp; a labeled, color-coded image. We can also&nbsp;make a 3-D model to understand a membrane, like this. It’s not a perfect representation of&nbsp; the membrane in reality. But that’s the thing, no model is. It’s just another&nbsp;way of wrapping your head —or your hands—around a concept&nbsp;that can be difficult to grasp. Scientists can also understand the&nbsp;membrane better by modeling how its molecules move mathematically. And mathematical&nbsp;models can zoom out way bigger than a cell. Computers can simulate experiments thousands of&nbsp; times, in ways that aren’t possible in real life. And that can help scientists predict and explain&nbsp;patterns, like how earthquakes could affect different places, what future weather may be,&nbsp; and even how diseases spread across populations. So, models aren’t perfect representations&nbsp;of reality. But they’re an important part of how we build and share knowledge. Because&nbsp;the sharing part is really important. A wise man once said, “The science isn’t&nbsp; finished until it’s communicated”. The scientific process helps us answer&nbsp; questions about the causes and effects of all sorts of stuff. But there are&nbsp;questions that may fall outside the scope of what science can prove or disprove. Questions about morality, for example. Like, science can answer the question, “Can&nbsp;we clone a mammoth that has been extinct for thousands of years?” But it can’t answer the&nbsp;question “Should we clone a mammoth that's Though I think Steven Spielberg gave us a pretty good answer to that question in the&nbsp;’90s. (You feel me? Jurassic Park anybody?) At the same time, science can join&nbsp;up with other ways of knowing — like philosophy and ethics— to grapple with&nbsp;questions neither field can answer alone. And scientific knowledge can also inform&nbsp; policy decisions, to get stuff done. Like, scientists can track wolf population&nbsp; numbers to identify threats that they’re facing. And that information can be used&nbsp; to create policies that protect them. So, science, as we know it today, may have&nbsp; only been around for a few hundred years, but the processes of discovery and&nbsp;knowledge collection are as old and diverse as humanity itself. Science&nbsp;proceeds in a more complicated way than the six simplified steps that&nbsp;we learned in elementary school. And it’s rarely a solo endeavor. It’s really a&nbsp; huge group effort—with scientists sharing ideas, checking each other’s work, and adding to a wider&nbsp; conversation about the observable physical world. Next time, we’ll dive deeper into&nbsp; the biologists’ corner of science, and the nitty-gritty details of how they&nbsp; study living things. I’ll see you then.   1. @crashcourse [215 likes]: Correction:
In this video, we conflate a hypothesis with a prediction. In science, a hypothesis is a tentative explanation for an observed phenomenon. It aims to answer: Why does something happen? A prediction, on the other hand, is a reasoned guess about what might happen if we test that hypothesis in an experiment. 

To revisit our egg example, a true scientific hypothesis might be: "Eggshells inhibit pressure from being released from eggs." We might test that hypothesis by microwaving eggs both with and without shells to see if pressure from the heat gets trapped, leading to explosion. If our hypothesis is correct, we predict that the shelled egg will explode and the shell-less egg will not. 

These two terms are often blended in textbooks, classrooms, and even at times by working scientists. But they are actually two separate, though closely linked, parts of the scientific process!

- Why Are My Video Intros And Outros Failing To Export Correctly? - Video And Design Saas Solutions: Kind: captions Language: en Why are my video intros and outros failing to export correctly? Imagine spending hours designing a perfect intro or outro only to find it looks terrible or won't export properly. That can be frustrating. But let's figure out what might be causing these issues. When you create intros and outros, these clips need to blend seamlessly with your main video. They often include motion graphics, text, and sometimes transparent backgrounds. The export process must keep their quality, timing, and effects intact. If something goes wrong, your video might turn pixelated, out of sync, or not export at all. One common reason is mismatched project settings. For example, if your intro is set to a resolution of 1920x 1080 pixels, but your main video is 30 at 40x 2160 pixels, the final export can look blurry or jittery. Make sure your project resolution and frame rate match your main video. Also, check the color space. If your intro uses a different color profile than your main footage, you might see color shifts or flickering. Another issue is codec compatibility. The codec is how your video is compressed. Some codecs support transparency, which is essential if your intro has overlays or lower thirds with see-through backgrounds. If your SAS platform doesn't support these codecs, transparent areas might turn black or white. Common professional codecs that support transparency include Apple ProRes and DNxHaged, but many tools limit your options. Bit rate is also important. Exporting at a low bit rate can make your graphics look blocky or pixelated, especially if your intro has detailed motion graphics. Increasing the bit rate improves quality, but can result in larger files. SAS platforms sometimes apply heavy compression to save bandwidth, which can hurt your visual quality. Software limitations can also cause problems. Some says editors are built for quick, simple projects. If your intro or outro has many layers, effects, or high resolution assets, the platform might struggle to process everything. Breaking your project into smaller parts, and rendering separately can help. Cache and performance issues are common, too. Temporary files or cached data can interfere with exporting. Clearing your cache or restarting the app often fixes these glitches. It's a good idea to test small clips during your editing process. Export short sections to see if they look right before doing a full render. When working in a SAS environment, remember that these tools are convenient, but may have limits. They might restrict codec options, bit rate controls, or project complexity. If your intros or outros are very complex, consider creating them in a dedicated motion graphics program like Adobe After Effects. Render the intro or outro there first, then import the finished file into your SAS editor for final assembly. Always preview your exported files before sharing or publishing. Check for sync issues, visual quality, and transparency. If problems keep happening, consult the platform's support resources or forums. They often have tips for troubleshooting common export issues. The main causes of failed exports are mismatch settings, codec limitations, excessive complexity, or platform restrictions. By matching your project settings, choosing the right export format, and understanding your SES platform's limits, you can get professionallook results. Testing often, and simplifying complex projects can save you time and frustration. If needed, use multiple tools to get the best quality for your intros and outros. This way, your videos will look sharp and fit perfectly with your main content every time.

- The benefits of good posture - Murat Dalkilinç: Kind: captions Language: en Has anyone ever told you, "Stand up straight!" or scolded you for slouching at a family dinner? Comments like that might be annoying, but they're not wrong. Your posture, the way you hold your body when you're sitting or standing, is the foundation for every movement your body makes, and can determine how well your body adapts to the stresses on it. These stresses can be things like carrying weight, or sitting in an awkward position. And the big one we all experience all day every day: gravity. If your posture isn't optimal, your muscles have to work harder to keep you upright and balanced. Some muscles will become tight and inflexbile. Others will be inhibited. Over time, these dysfunctional adaptations impair your body's ability to deal with the forces on it. Poor posture inflicts extra wear and tear on your joints and ligaments, increases the likelihood of accidents, and makes some organs, like your lungs, less efficient. Researchers have linked poor posture to scoliosis, tension headaches, and back pain, though it isn't the exclusive cause of any of them. Posture can even influence your emotional state and your sensitivity to pain. So there are a lot of reasons to aim for good posture. But it's getting harder these days. Sitting in an awkward position for a long time can promote poor posture, and so can using computers or mobile devices, which encourage you to look downward. Many studies suggest that, on average, posture is getting worse. So what does good posture look like? When you look at the spine from the front or the back, all 33 vertebrae should appear stacked in a straight line. From the side, the spine should have three curves: one at your neck, one at your shoulders, and one at the small of your back. You aren't born with this s-shaped spine. Babies' spines just have one curve like a "c." The other curves usually develop by 12-18 months as the muscles strengthen. These curves help us stay upright and absorb some of the stress from activities like walking and jumping. If they are aligned properly, when you're standing up, you should be able to draw a straight line from a point just in front of your shoulders, to behind your hip, to the front of your knee, to a few inches in front of your ankle. This keeps your center of gravity directly over your base of support, which allows you to move efficiently with the least amount of fatigue and muscle strain. If you're sitting, your neck should be vertical, not tilted forward. Your shoulders should be relaxed with your arms close to your trunk. Your knees should be at a right angle with your feet flat on the floor. But what if your posture isn't that great? Try redesigning your environment. Adjust your screen so it's at or slightly below eyelevel. Make sure all parts of your body, like your elbows and wrists, are supported, using ergonomic aids if you need to. Try sleeping on your side with your neck supported and with a pillow between your legs. Wear shoes with low heels and good arch support, and use a headset for phone calls. It's also not enough to just have good posture. Keeping your muscles and joints moving is extremely important. In fact, being stationary for long periods with good posture can be worse than regular movement with bad posture. When you do move, move smartly. Keep anything you're carrying close to your body. Backpacks should be in contact with your back carried symetrically. If you sit a lot, get up and move around on occassion, and be sure to exercise. Using your muscles will keep them strong enough to support you effectively, on top of all the other benefits to your joints, bones, brain and heart. And if you're really worried, check with a physical therapist, because yes, you really should stand up straight.

Start the video with emotion. Like, write that down or get that tattooed or something cuz even that alone will change everything for you. Because at the end of the day, we are highly emotional creatures. Because even when we're just browsing YouTube and we think our brains are turned off, there's still a lot of subconscious emotional stuff going on. So, that's why the very first thing that our videos need to do is to create that emotional interruption. But how do we actually do this? Because sure, if you're watching that Netflix show and you get to that cliffhanger, of course you're going to feel emotional. You know, you're invested in the characters, you're invested in the story line, but how do we create that same feeling in the hook of our videos? Like, how is that even possible? Well, luckily, there's a few ways to do this, but my absolute favorite and the one I keep coming back to is to create a one sentence story. So, let's break this down. I think the single most powerful technique for creating emotion in your videos is storytelling. But we can't start off a video with a long rambly story because it just takes too long and it just kills any curiosity. But what we can do is start the video by condensing an emotionally charged story into a single sentence. Because this way, what you're doing is giving the viewer just enough context to get them hooked and create that emotional tension. And that tension is what keeps them watching. And I can even give you an example from my own journey. So, the video that took this channel from getting literally two views a day to this actually used that one sentence story method. Creating content completely changed my life in just 90 days. And that was the first sentence of the video and it gets the viewer asking a lot of questions. How did it change your life in 90 days? You know, how is that even possible? And then they end up watching the rest of the video to answer those questions. And this becomes so effective because now that we've triggered their emotions, we can then move on to the second part of the chain reaction hook, which is the promise. Now, this second part of the hook is so unbelievably simple, but it is crucial that you get it right. Because once you've triggered their emotion, we need to give the logical part of their brain a reason to stick around as well. And it's actually really simple. All you need to do is give them a concrete, tangible promise of what they're going to get out of the video. And this is actually something that all of the successful creators understand very well. In this video, we're going to be discussing a simple three-step method that you can use to totally transform your life in the next 90 days. So, today I'm going to show you how you can replicate the wealthiest people's exact steps and make money work for you. But how do we apply this to your videos? Well, the easiest way to do this is to say something like, "So, in this video, I'll give you X." Or, "In this video, I'm going to reveal the secret to X." or something like, "And by the end of this video, you're going to have everything you need to start and then just whatever the video is about." And we want to keep it short. We want to keep it specific and just make sure that they know exactly what they're going to get out of the video. Because if your promise is clear and compelling enough and you've already hooked them emotionally, that is a killer hook right there. And I literally give a promise like this in every single video. But in this video, I'm going to show you. So, in this video, I want to share with you. And in this video, I'm going to break down. And the reason I do it is because it just works wonders. However, there is still one last piece of the puzzle because the third and final part of the chain reaction hook is something I call the value transition. Now, this is so interesting because I never hear any YouTube experts talking about this, but I see it in so many high-erforming videos. It's crazy. And that is that right after you've made that promise, you need to give your viewer some sort of confirmation that you're about to deliver the value that you just promised. Because now we've built up all this momentum in the hook. We've created these emotional triggers and we've given them this big promise. Now, we just need to keep that momentum going. Because if your viewer thinks that they might have to wait for ages until they get the thing that they clicked onto the video for, then they're just going to click off the video. They're just going to get bored. So, how do we actually do this? How do we bridge the gap between the hook and the main section of the video? So, the value in the video. Well, one very easy, very beginner friendly way to do this is to use a very simple title text screen. So, let's say you've just promised your viewer that you're going to give them 10 brutally honest tips about how to lose body fat or something like that. You can then hit them with, okay, so the first brutally honest tip is to and then just get straight into the video. And this way, you're kind of saying to your viewer, right, no more messing around. The video is starting. And you're basically saying that I'm about to give you the exact thing that I just promised you. And finally, I know I've thrown a lot at you there. So, let's bring this all together by watching an example from one of my favorite YouTubers at the moment called Nisha. And this is actually her most viewed video. So I'm not just cherry-picking. So yeah, let's have a watch. I have spent the last decade of my life immersing myself in the field of finance and money through a degree in finance, a qualification in accounting, and then a career in investment banking. And one of the most life-changing skills I have learned through it all is how to handle my own finances, recognize my bad money habits, and break free from them. So in this video, I'm going to share with you nine of the most common bad money habits that hold people back, and tips on how to break out of them. Number one, paying yourself last. And I hope you can see how perfectly that fit the structure. So, this chain reaction idea and yeah, that video has 10 million views. So, clearly it worked. So, now that we've looked at the three steps to create an irresistible hook, I actually want to dive into something equally important, which is what not to do in your hooks. And I've actually got a few of these, so we're just going to rapid fire through them. So, number one is assuming your viewer already cares. And this might sound a little bit harsh, but just because you care about the topic of a video doesn't mean that your viewer does. Because someone watching your video doesn't owe you their attention. You have to earn it. And as you now know, the best way to earn a viewer's attention is to give them a clear and compelling promise and then actually deliver on that promise. Now, the second thing that you don't want to do in your hooks is saying it but not showing it. Now, if you remember the example I just gave when Nisha was telling her one-s sentence story, she edited in images of her getting her degree and speaking on stage. And this massively builds trust all in the first few seconds of the video because it just backs up what she's saying. So if you are telling a story about your life or a certain achievement or a certain experience you've had, you want to ask yourself, can I also show this instead of just saying it? Now the third thing that you never want to do in your hooks is solving the puzzle too early. So remember that when it comes to your hooks, curiosity is key. That is the main emotion that we want to trigger. But if your hook already answers all the big questions in the video, then people will have no reason to keep watching because you haven't created any curiosity. And the fourth thing to never do when it comes to your hooks is making it about you instead of them. Now, I believe the single best piece of advice when it comes to content creation in general is to switch your mindset from how can I get more views to how can I be more valuable? But that mindset shift is especially important in our hooks because when someone clicks onto your videos, they are basically thinking is this video even worth my time? So, your job is to answer that question immediately in the hook, which is exactly why that promise part of the chain reaction hook is so powerful because when people feel like a video is made for them, they will stick around. It's as simple as that.   20. @raakgu: She's misunderstanding the retention metric and the swipe away metric.

Swipe away means did the user swipe past without watching your Short.

Retention means out of only those people who began watching your Short, what percentage of the video length did they make it to before swiping away.

The retention can be greater than 100% if your average viewer watches your video into the loop of it starting over.

Not because it relates to swipe away metric in any way.
